1.html:
Secondary hardening is the rise in hardness, after the normal softening, when a quenched steel containing strong carbide formers (Mo, V, W, Cr) is tempered at about 500 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}.

  • Up to about 400^\circ\mathrm{C} cementite precipitates and coarsens, so hardness falls.
  • At 500 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C} the substitutional alloy atoms can diffuse, and a very fine, coherent dispersion of alloy carbides (\mathrm{Mo_2C}, VC, \mathrm{W_2C}) forms on the dislocations of the martensite. These replace cementite and pin dislocations, so hardness rises again, sometimes above the as-quenched value.
  • Retained austenite also turns to fresh martensite on cooling from the tempering temperature, so tool steels are double tempered.
  • Above about 650^\circ\mathrm{C} the carbides coarsen and hardness drops (overaging).

This gives the red hardness of high speed and hot-work tool steels.

Mo and hardenability. Dissolved Mo delays the diffusional ferrite and pearlite reactions much more than the bainite reaction. The pearlite nose moves to longer times and a bay opens between the pearlite and bainite C-curves, so thick sections harden through or form bainite on air cooling. Mo must be dissolved in austenite; undissolved Mo carbides lower hardenability.

Mo and mechanical properties.

PropertyEffect of MoTypical value
Hardenabilitydelays ferrite and pearlite, bainite bayf_{\mathrm{Mo}} \approx 1 + 3.0\,(\%\mathrm{Mo}), about 2.5 at 0.5\% Mo
Tempering resistancefine \mathrm{Mo_2C}, secondary hardening peakM2 high speed steel about 64 HRC after tempering at 550^\circ\mathrm{C}
Toughnessreduces temper embrittlement0.2 to 0.5\% Mo
Hot and creep strengthsolid solution in ferrite plus stable carbides0.5Mo and 2.25Cr-1Mo boiler steels

Mo therefore gives deep, uniform hardening, resistance to softening and better toughness after tempering, as in 4140, 4340 and M2 steels.

Notes that Mo must be dissolved in austenite; undissolved carbides lower hardenability

With M in kg, C in \mathrm{kcal/(kg\,^\circ C)} and \Delta T in ^\circ\mathrm{C}, the product is an energy in kJ (kW s), not a power; dividing by the heating time gives the power, 72.72\ \mathrm{kJ} / 2\ \mathrm{s} = 36.36 kW, which is what the slide's last step does. \Delta T is the temperature rise, not the surface temperature itself.
10.html:
Induction heating

Induction heating is non-contact heating of an electrically conducting part placed in or near a water-cooled copper coil carrying high-frequency alternating current. The alternating magnetic field induces eddy currents in the part, and their Joule (I^2R) heating, plus hysteresis loss below the Curie point (770^\circ\mathrm{C}), heats it. The current crowds into a surface layer (skin effect) of depth

\delta = 5.03\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\mu f}}\ \mathrm{cm}

so a higher frequency heats a thinner layer. For hardening, this layer is austenitised in seconds and spray-quenched to martensite, while the core stays tough.

Power capacity

Given: round bar, diameter 25 mm (printed "25 in"; see Watch out), length 50 mm; hardened depth 1.5 mm over the whole circumference and length; heating time t = 2 s.

Assumed: steel density 7.85\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}; average specific heat C = 0.15\ \mathrm{kcal/(kg\,^\circ C)} (0.63\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}); heated from room temperature to about 920^\circ\mathrm{C}, so \Delta T \approx 900^\circ\mathrm{C}; total heat supplied = 3 times the heat absorbed (slide 40).

Find: generator power P (kW).

Step 1. Mass of the hardened shell (inner diameter 25 - 2(1.5) = 22 mm):

\begin{aligned} V &= \frac{\pi}{4}\left(25^2 - 22^2\right)(50) = 5537\ \mathrm{mm^3} = 5.54\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ M &= 5.54 \times 7.85 = 43.5\ \mathrm{g} = 0.0435\ \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

Step 2. Heat absorbed (the P_1 term):

E_1 = 4.186\,M C \Delta T = 4.186 \times 0.0435 \times 0.15 \times 900 = 24.6\ \mathrm{kJ}

Step 3. Losses. Radiation, convection, coil and coupling losses, and above all conduction into the core: in 2 s heat diffuses about \sqrt{\alpha t} \approx 3.7 mm, more than the case. These are hard to calculate, so practice takes

E = 3E_1 = 3 \times 24.6 = 73.7\ \mathrm{kJ}

Step 4. Power:

P = \frac{E}{t} = \frac{73.7\ \mathrm{kJ}}{2\ \mathrm{s}} = 36.8\ \mathrm{kW}

over a surface of \pi(2.5)(5.0) = 39.3\ \mathrm{cm^2}, about 0.94\ \mathrm{kW/cm^2}.

Answer: about 37 kW (the slide's mass of 0.0429 kg gives 36.4 kW); a generator of about 40 kW.
pts: Definition: AC in a water-cooled copper coil induces eddy currents in the part; Joule heating, no contact
Skin effect: current and heat in a surface layer \delta = 5.03\sqrt{\rho/\mu f}, thinner at higher frequency; hysteresis below the Curie point
Hardening use: surface austenitised in seconds and quenched, tough core
Reads the diameter as 25 mm and states the assumptions (density, C = 0.15 kcal/kg C, \Delta T \approx 900^\circ\mathrm{C})
Shell volume \frac{\pi}{4}(25^2 - 22^2)(50) = 5537\ \mathrm{mm^3} and M \approx 0.0435 kg
E_1 = 4.186\,MC\Delta T \approx 24.6 kJ
Total heat 3E_1 \approx 73.7 kJ, with the reason (losses, mainly conduction into the core)
P = 73.7/2 \approx 37 kW, unit kW
Comment: about 0.94 kW/cm², generator of about 40 kW

11.html:
Effects of alloying elements (slides 4-5; book pp 293-295)

Alloying elements act on cast iron mainly through the graphite-cementite balance and the matrix, somewhat differently from steel:

ElementEffect
Si (1 to 3%)graphitiser; promotes a ferritic matrix and oxidation resistance; but lowers impact energy and thermal conductivity and raises the DBTT
Sas FeS promotes cementite (chill); must be balanced by Mn; kept below about 0.02% in ductile iron before Mg treatment
Mnfirst forms MnS (1.7\,\%\mathrm{S}); free Mn resists graphitisation and promotes pearlite: 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.15 for maximum ferrite, 3\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.35 for pearlite
Phardly changes the graphite-cementite ratio; forms low-melting steadite; kept low against shrinkage porosity, cold shortness and low ductility
Cu (0.4 to 0.8%)strong pearlite promoter; raises proof stress, UTS and hardness without embrittling
Ni (0.5 to 2%)mild graphitiser; strengthens ferrite and raises UTS without loss of impact energy; embrittles in large additions
Momild pearlite promoter; raises YS, hardness, hardenability and high-temperature strength; reduces temper embrittlement; intercellular carbides in heavy sections
Crcorrosion and oxidation resistance, but a strong carbide former, so avoided where a carbide-free structure is needed

Carbide formers are the main danger (slide 5). Massive carbide gives shrinkage porosity, cracking in fettling, poor ductility, impact strength and machinability, and needs high-temperature annealing to remove.

Compositional requirement for grey iron

  1. C 2.5 to 4.0% and Si 1 to 3% (slide 6). On the C-Si map this lies above \%\mathrm{C} + \tfrac{1}{6}\%\mathrm{Si} = 2.0 and at or below the eutectic, \%\mathrm{C} + \tfrac{1}{3}\%\mathrm{Si} = 4.3. The carbon equivalent, \mathrm{CE} = \%\mathrm{C} + (\%\mathrm{Si} + \%\mathrm{P})/3, must be high enough (about 3.6 to 4.3) for the section's cooling rate; low CE or thin sections freeze white.
  2. Mn balanced against S: at least 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S}, from about 0.1% Mn for ferritic up to 1.2% for pearlitic grades.
  3. S and P moderate: S about 0.05 to 0.15%, not removed as Mg would remove it in ductile iron, so that S and O keep the graphite as flakes; P below about 0.3%.
  4. No spheroidisers (Mg, Ce) and few carbide formers (Cr, V), plus inoculation with FeSi so that graphite nucleates.

S and Mn: FeS promotes cementite; Mn forms MnS first; free Mn promotes pearlite, with the 1.7S, 1.7S + 0.15 and 3S + 0.35 rules
P: steadite, shrinkage porosity, cold shortness; kept low
Cu, Ni and Mo: Cu strong pearlite promoter; Ni strength without loss of impact; Mo strength, high-temperature properties and less temper embrittlement
Cr: corrosion resistance but strong carbide former; carbides cause porosity, fettling cracks and poor machinability
Grey iron needs C 2.5 to 4.0% and Si 1 to 3%, with CE near but below the eutectic 4.3, matched to the section
Mn of 0.1 to 1.2%, balanced against S; S and P at moderate levels
No Mg or Ce, few carbide formers, inoculation with FeSi

12.html:
Annealing practices (slide 10; book pp 299-301)

Annealing softens ductile iron by producing a carbide-free, fully ferritic matrix. The aims are maximum ductility and toughness, better machinability and uniform properties, to grades 60-45-12 and 60-40-18.

TypeUseHeatingCooling
Low-temperature (ferritising)carbide-free iron720 to 730^\circ\mathrm{C}, 1 h per inch of sectionfurnace cool at 55^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}, air cool
Fulllower-Si iron, 60-40-18 with maximum low-temperature impact870 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, only to equalisefurnace cool at 55^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}, air cool
High-temperature (graphitising)carbides present900 to 925^\circ\mathrm{C}, at least 2 hfurnace cool at 95^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}, then 55^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}, air cool
Two-stagecarbides present, fast cooling practical870 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, 1 h per inchfast cool to 675 to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}, hold at 730^\circ\mathrm{C} for 2 h per inch, air cool

How they work. Below the critical range, pearlitic cementite decomposes and its carbon diffuses to the nodules, leaving ferrite; the time grows as the nodule count falls. Above it, eutectic carbide dissolves in the austenite (the rate doubles for every 55^\circ\mathrm{C}, slide 7). Slow cooling through the critical range (about 790 to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}) then lets carbon deposit on the nodules, so the austenite becomes ferrite instead of pearlite.

Graphitespheroidsthe same spheroids, slightly larger
Matrixpearlite with ferrite rings around the nodules (bull's eye); thin sections may hold eutectic carbideequiaxed ferrite grains; no pearlite or carbide
Propertiesstronger and harder: 488 to 804 MPa UTS at 8 to 15% elongation for 40 to 100% pearlite (slide 12)softer: about 415 MPa UTS but 12 to 18% elongation; best toughness and machinability

The bull's eye forms because, on cooling through the eutectoid, carbon next to each nodule diffuses onto the graphite and the carbon-depleted ring becomes ferrite. So an as-cast iron is never fully pearlitic.

Mechanism: carbide dissolves or decomposes and its carbon moves to the nodules; slow cooling through the critical range gives ferrite

13.html:
Heat-treatment cycle (slide 16)

  1. Casting and hot working. The ingot (or PM compact) is forged or rolled in the austenite + carbide field, below the upper forging limit (slide 17), to break up the cast carbide network, then air cooled.
  2. Normalising. Heat into the austenite + carbide field, about 50^\circ\mathrm{C} above Ac3 (towards Acm for high carbon), and air cool: uniform fine grain and dissolution of grain-boundary carbides. It is skipped for air-hardening high-alloy grades, which would form martensite and crack.
  3. Annealing (spheroidising). Heat just above Ac1 (austenite + ferrite + carbide field) and cool very slowly, about 10^\circ\mathrm{C/h}: soft ferrite with globular carbides, ready for machining.
  4. Machining to near-final shape, because hardened tool steel can only be ground or spark eroded (EDM).
  5. Stress relief. Below Ac1, about 550 to 620^\circ\mathrm{C}, for 1 to 2 h, cooling at most 300^\circ\mathrm{C/h}: recovery removes machining stresses without changing the microstructure, so the tool distorts less on hardening.
  6. Hardening.
    • Preheat high-alloy grades (CE above 0.7): for HSS at 500 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C} and 850^\circ\mathrm{C} (slide 30).
    • Austenitise: about 30 min per 25 mm at 750 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C} for low-alloy steels; about 1200 to 1290^\circ\mathrm{C}, close to the solidus, for HSS, for a short, controlled time in a salt bath or vacuum, to dissolve enough carbide without grain growth or decarburisation.
    • Quench in water, oil, salt (450 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C} for HSS) or air, according to hardenability.
    • Temper at once: 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} for carbon steels; two or three times at 540 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C} for HSS.
  7. Finish grinding to final size.

Purposes of heat treatment

  • A machinable or cold-formable structure (annealing).
  • Relief of residual stresses from forming, machining and grinding.
  • A homogeneous structure with fine globular carbides.
  • Dissolution of intergranular carbides and grain refinement (normalising).
  • Hardness and wear resistance from martensite with the right amount and type of carbide.
  • Tempering: removal of retained austenite, fine controlled carbides (secondary hardening, red hardness), toughness and dimensional stability.

Machining before hardening; grinding or EDM after
Stress relief below Ac1 (about 550 to 620 degrees C) by recovery, slow cooling, no microstructural change
Hardening: preheating, austenitising temperature and time (750 to 900 degrees C low alloy, near solidus for HSS), protection from decarburisation, quench medium by hardenability
Tempering at once: low for carbon steels, two or three times at 540 to 570 degrees C for HSS

14.html:
Transformation steps (slides 25-26)

As-quenched tool steel is martensite, retained austenite (RA) and undissolved carbides. Tempering below Ac1 runs in three steps for carbon steels and five for highly alloyed tool steels:

  1. 50 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C}: fine coherent \varepsilon-carbide (\mathrm{Fe_{2.4}C}) precipitates from the martensite and tetragonality falls; volume contracts; softening is delayed.
  2. 200 to 350^\circ\mathrm{C}: \varepsilon-carbide dissolves and \mathrm{Fe_3C} precipitates as rods and films at the lath boundaries; the matrix becomes ferrite; hardness falls.
  3. RA destabilisation (from about 150^\circ\mathrm{C} in carbon steels, 450^\circ\mathrm{C} in high-alloy steels): carbides precipitate from the RA and its M_s rises; it becomes bainite, or fresh martensite on cooling, with a volume expansion.
  4. From about 500^\circ\mathrm{C} (high-alloy steels): carbon passes from cementite to fine alloy carbides (\mathrm{M_2C} and MC of Mo, W, V), giving secondary hardening and a large expansion (slide 26).
  5. 600^\circ\mathrm{C} to Ac1: carbides coalesce and coarsen and the matrix recovers; softening and contraction.

Effect of tempering temperature on hardness (slides 27-28)

  • Class 1, carbon and low-alloy steels: hardness falls continuously, slowly to about 200^\circ\mathrm{C}, then steeply as cementite coarsens (a eutectoid steel tempered 1 h: about 61 HRC at 205^\circ\mathrm{C}, 39 HRC at 535^\circ\mathrm{C}).
  • Class 2, cold-work alloy steels (A, D): the alloy retards carbide precipitation: a plateau (D2 holds to about 425^\circ\mathrm{C}), then a drop.
  • Class 3, high-speed steels: martensite softening is offset by RA transformation and alloy-carbide precipitation, so hardness rises to a secondary peak at about 500 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C} that can exceed the as-quenched value (about 64.5 against 63.5 HRC, book Fig 4.31), then falls steeply above about 600^\circ\mathrm{C} as the carbides coarsen.
  • Class 4, hot-work steels: lower start (less carbon), then a mild secondary hump.

Time matters as well as temperature: the tempering parameter T(c + \log t) (T in K, t in h, c about 20) combines them, so a higher temperature for a shorter time gives the same hardness.

15.html:
What duplex steel is

Duplex (austenitic-ferritic) stainless steel has two phases in roughly equal amounts: ferrite (\alpha, BCC) and austenite (\gamma, FCC). Compared with 304 or 316 it has more Cr (20 to 28%) and Mo (up to 5%), less Ni (up to 9%) and 0.05 to 0.50% N. Grades: lean (2101, 2304), standard (2205: 22Cr-5Ni-3Mo-0.15N) and super duplex (2507). On the Schaeffler diagram it lies in the "duplex alloys" field between the austenitic and ferritic fields.

How the structure forms

It solidifies as ferrite; austenite forms in the solid state near 1300^\circ\mathrm{C}, first at ferrite boundaries. Hot working at 1000 to 1200^\circ\mathrm{C} gives alternating \alpha/\gamma lamellae. Solution annealing at about 1050^\circ\mathrm{C} and water quenching fix about 50/50 (minor phase not below 30%). Cr, Mo and Si concentrate in ferrite, Ni and N in austenite.

Feature of the structureProperty

16.html:
Why PH steels are superior to Fe-Cr-C martensitic steels

  1. Different source of strength. Fe-Cr-C martensite owes its strength to carbon (up to 1.2% C) in BCT martensite and carbides; more C gives brittle plate martensite, retained austenite and low toughness. PH steels keep C at or below about 0.07%: the matrix is soft, tough lath martensite (or austenite), and the strength comes from nanometre intermetallic or Cu precipitates (NiAl, \mathrm{Ni_3Al}, \mathrm{Ni_3Ti}, Cu). YS reaches about 1700 MPa with better ductility and toughness.
  2. Stable precipitates. Coherent, uniformly spread particles pin dislocations, and they resist overaging: NiAl is still about 7 nm after 4 h at 625^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  3. Better corrosion resistance. With little carbon, Cr is not tied up in carbides; Ti and Nb bind C and N as MC and M(C,N), and dissolved Cu helps. Martensitic Fe-Cr-C grades are the least corrosion resistant stainless steels.
  4. Easier processing. Parts are machined soft and then aged at 480 to 620^\circ\mathrm{C} with no quench: little distortion, cracking or decarburisation; low C also aids welding. Fe-Cr-C grades need austenitising at 950 to 1100^\circ\mathrm{C}, quenching, subzero treatment and tempering outside 420 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Heat treatment of PH steels

Martensitic (single treatment: 17-4 PH, 15-5 PH, Custom 450)

  1. Solution anneal at about 1040^\circ\mathrm{C} (980 to 1065^\circ\mathrm{C}; Condition A) and cool fast: martensite with no retained austenite, supersaturated in Cu.
  2. Age at 480 to 620^\circ\mathrm{C} for 1 to 4 h: 17-4 PH reaches a tensile strength of about 1310 MPa (YS about 1170 MPa) after 1 h at 480^\circ\mathrm{C}, or 930 MPa (YS about 725 MPa) with more toughness after 4 h at 620^\circ\mathrm{C} (overaged).

Semi-austenitic (double treatment: 17-7 PH)

  1. Solution anneal at 1065^\circ\mathrm{C} and quench: austenite, easy to form.
  2. Condition at about 760^\circ\mathrm{C}: \mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6} precipitates, taking C and Cr out of the austenite and raising M_s; cool below 15^\circ\mathrm{C} to form martensite. Alternatively condition at 955^\circ\mathrm{C} (fewer carbides) and transform by a subzero treatment at -75^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  3. Age at 565 to 595^\circ\mathrm{C} (after the 760^\circ\mathrm{C} route): NiAl and \mathrm{Ni_3Al} give UTS 1030 to 1240 MPa.

Aging is set at peak strength or slightly overaged (better hydrogen-embrittlement resistance).

2.html:
Tool steel for a cold-forming die: AISI D2, the high-carbon high-chromium cold-work steel (about 1.5% C, 12% Cr, 0.9% Mo, 1.0% V).

A cold-forming die works below about 200^\circ\mathrm{C} but under high contact pressure and sliding of the work, so it needs:

  • high hardness (58 to 62 HRC) and compressive strength, so the die face does not sink;
  • high wear (abrasion) resistance for long runs;
  • enough toughness to resist chipping;
  • deep hardening with minimum distortion, because dies are large and finished to close tolerances.

Red hardness is not needed.

Why D2:

  • A large volume of hard \mathrm{M_7C_3} chromium carbides gives excellent wear resistance.
  • 12% Cr with Mo gives so much hardenability that the die hardens by air cooling from about 1010^\circ\mathrm{C}: low quench stress, very little distortion, no cracking ("non-deforming").
  • Tempering at about 200^\circ\mathrm{C} gives about 60 to 62 HRC; double tempering near 500^\circ\mathrm{C} (secondary hardening) gives about 58 HRC with better stability.
  • Examples: blanking, cold-forming and drawing dies, thread-rolling dies, slitter blades, forming rolls.

Alternatives: A2 (1% C, 5% Cr, 1% Mo, air hardening) when the die takes some impact; O1 (oil quenched from about 800^\circ\mathrm{C}, tempered below 200^\circ\mathrm{C}) for short runs and small dies. W grades need a water quench and crack, so they are avoided.

Dual-phase C-Mn steels (about 0.06 to 0.15% C, 1.0 to 1.5% Mn) are annealed in the \alpha + \gamma range (about 760 to 800^\circ\mathrm{C}) and cooled fast enough for the carbon-rich austenite islands to become martensite; Mn supplies the hardenability. The result is 20 to 30% martensite in soft, fine-grained ferrite. Inherent qualities:

  • Continuous yielding: no yield-point elongation or Luders bands, because the expansion of the martensite leaves mobile dislocations in the ferrite around it.
  • Low YS/UTS ratio, about 0.5, with a high UTS (500 to 1000 MPa).
  • High initial work-hardening rate: strong resistance to necking, large uniform strain and superior formability for the strength.
  • Good bake hardening, fatigue strength and crash-energy absorption; lean, low-carbon composition gives good weldability.
  • Example: DP600 for car pillars, rails and wheels.

3.fix: Slides 74 and 77 of 401-ch1 write the eutectic as "One Liquid (4.3%C) ⇔ Fe3C + Ledeburite", and page 79 of the course book says two solids, "cementite and ledeburite", form. Ledeburite is itself the eutectic mixture of austenite and cementite, so it cannot be a product beside cementite. The correct reaction is \mathrm{L}\ (4.3\%\ \mathrm{C}) \to \gamma\ (2.11\ \text{to}\ 2.14\%\ \mathrm{C}) + \mathrm{Fe_3C}\ (6.67\%\ \mathrm{C}), which is the boxed equation on slide 77 itself.
3.html:
Eutectic reaction. An invariant reaction in which one liquid changes, at constant temperature on cooling, into two different solids (and back on heating). In the Fe-\mathrm{Fe_3C} diagram it occurs at 1147^\circ\mathrm{C}:

\mathrm{L}\ (4.3\%\ \mathrm{C}) \;\rightleftharpoons\; \gamma\ (2.14\%\ \mathrm{C}) + \mathrm{Fe_3C}\ (6.67\%\ \mathrm{C})

The \gamma + \mathrm{Fe_3C} eutectic mixture is ledeburite, about 52% austenite and 48% cementite by the lever rule. Cast irons (2.14 to 6.67% C) undergo it; below 727^\circ\mathrm{C} its austenite becomes pearlite (transformed ledeburite).

Cementite network in a hypereutectoid steel (1.1% C, slow cooling):

  1. Above A_{cm} (about 830^\circ\mathrm{C} for 1.1% C): uniform austenite grains, all carbon in solution.
  2. At A_{cm}: the austenite is saturated with carbon. Proeutectoid \mathrm{Fe_3C} nucleates at the austenite grain boundaries, the high-energy sites and fast diffusion paths.
  3. Between A_{cm} and A_1: carbon diffuses to the boundaries and the cementite grows along them into a continuous film round every grain. The remaining austenite loses carbon along A_{cm} and reaches 0.76% C at 727^\circ\mathrm{C}. Lever rule: proeutectoid \mathrm{Fe_3C} = (1.10 - 0.76)/(6.67 - 0.76) = 5.8\%.
  4. At A_1 (727^\circ\mathrm{C}): the enclosed austenite undergoes the eutectoid reaction, \gamma\ (0.76\%) \to \alpha + \mathrm{Fe_3C}, forming lamellar pearlite (eutectoid ferrite + eutectoid cementite) inside each cell; the boundary cementite is unchanged.
  5. Down to room temperature: practically no change; ferrite only rejects a trace of carbon (0.022 to 0.008%).

Result: pearlite grains enclosed by a continuous proeutectoid cementite network (about 94% pearlite, 6% network). The hard, brittle network is a crack path, so it is broken up by normalising or spheroidising before service.

4.html:
Why annealing restores the corrosion resistance of cold-worked austenitic stainless steel

  1. Strain-induced martensite. Cold work turns part of the metastable austenite into \alpha^{\prime} martensite (BCC, ferromagnetic), so the steel becomes two-phase and partly magnetic. The martensite is less noble than the austenite, and the pair forms galvanic micro-cells.
  2. Stored energy and stress. High dislocation density, slip bands and residual tension remain. Slip steps break the thin \mathrm{Cr_2O_3} passive film and the strained sites act as anodes, so pitting and general attack increase (slide 11 micrographs). Residual tension also invites chloride stress-corrosion cracking.
  3. Annealing (solution annealing, 1010 to 1120^\circ\mathrm{C}, fast cooling) reverts the martensite to austenite, recrystallises the grains, removes the stresses and dissolves any Cr carbides. The result is uniform austenite with all its Cr in solution and a continuous passive film. Fast cooling through about 450 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C} prevents \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} sensitisation; for the same reason stress relief is done below 480^\circ\mathrm{C} or above 900^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Full-annealing schedule for the cast block

Given: C 0.8, Si 0.3, Mn 1.6, Ni 2.0, Cr 8.0, Mo 0.6 wt%. Find: temperature, soak and cooling.

Critical temperatures:

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{A_1} &= 723 - 10.7(1.6) - 16.9(2.0) + 29.1(0.3) + 16.9(8.0) = 816^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ \mathrm{A_3} &= 910 - 203\sqrt{0.8} - 15.2(2.0) + 44.7(0.3) + 31.5(0.6) = 730^\circ\mathrm{C} \end{aligned}

(The printed course forms, 20.7 \times \%\mathrm{Mn} and 203 \times \%\mathrm{C}, give \mathrm{A_1} = 800^\circ\mathrm{C} and \mathrm{A_3} = 750^\circ\mathrm{C}.) \mathrm{A_3} falls below \mathrm{A_1}: there is no ferrite-austenite range. 8% Cr, with Mn and Ni, moves the eutectoid carbon well below 0.8%, so this steel is hypereutectoid, and the rule is \mathrm{A_1} + 30 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C}:

T_{\text{anneal}} = 846\ \text{to}\ 866^\circ\mathrm{C}\ (830\ \text{to}\ 850\ \text{printed}), \quad \text{take } 850^\circ\mathrm{C}

Schedule:

  1. Heat slowly. A cast block holds casting stresses, and the Cr term alone gives a carbon equivalent of 8/4 = 2, far above 0.7: very crack-sensitive. Heat slowly through 250 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}, equalise at about 600 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}, then go to 850^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Soak 20 min per cm of the thickest section once the core is at temperature (200 min for a 100 mm block): austenite plus undissolved alloy carbides.
  3. Cool very slowly. Cr, Mn, Ni and Mo give very high hardenability, so normal cooling could form bainite or martensite. Furnace cool at the slow end, about 20^\circ\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}} or less, to about 600^\circ\mathrm{C} (about 12 h), then air cool.

Answer: anneal at about 850^\circ\mathrm{C} (\mathrm{A_1} \approx 816^\circ\mathrm{C}; 800 with the printed coefficient), 20 min per cm, furnace cool at most 20^\circ\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}} to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}; result: spheroidal alloy carbides in ferrite, soft and machinable.

5.html:
Benefits of normalising before hardening a critical-shape part

A critical shape (thick and thin sections, sharp corners, holes, keyways) concentrates the quench stresses, so any pre-existing stress or uneven structure ends as distortion or a crack. Normalising before hardening:

  1. Relieves residual stresses from forging, casting, machining or welding, so they do not add to the quench stresses.
  2. Refines and equalises the grain size, removing coarse as-cast, overheated or Widmanstätten structures. Fine prior grains give fine austenite and tougher, less crack-sensitive martensite.
  3. Homogenises the structure and removes banding, so every region austenitises, transforms and changes size alike: a consistent hardness and predictable growth or warpage. Gear blanks are normalised before machining and hardening for this reason.
  4. Gives fine, uniform pearlite and breaks any cementite network. Short diffusion distances let austenite form and homogenise quickly, so the hardening soak is short, with less grain growth, oxidation and decarburisation.
  5. Improves machinability and dimensional stability for the machining done before hardening.

Austenitisation mechanisms

Austenite forms by nucleation and growth controlled by carbon diffusion. After an incubation time it grows faster at higher temperature: for 0.8% C steel about half is transformed after roughly 10 s at 751^\circ\mathrm{C} but about 50 s at 730^\circ\mathrm{C} (slide 34). Several austenite grains form from one pearlite colony, so the new austenite is fine; a further hold is needed to even out the carbon.

  • Pearlitic steel: nuclei form mainly at the intersections of pearlite colonies and also at ferrite-cementite lamellar interfaces. The diffusion distance is only about half the interlamellar spacing, so austenitisation is fastest.
  • Spheroidised steel: nuclei form at the ferrite-carbide interfaces, first at particles on ferrite grain boundaries. Austenite grows as a shell round each particle while the carbide dissolves. Carbon must travel the inter-particle spacing, so the process is slower, and carbides may stay undissolved, which can be useful in hypereutectoid hardening.
  • Ferritic steel (low carbon, or the proeutectoid ferrite of a hypoeutectoid steel): nuclei form at ferrite grain boundaries, mainly triple junctions. With almost no carbon nearby, the ferrite is consumed only above \mathrm{Ac_3} or by austenite growing in from the carbon-rich pearlite regions, with long diffusion paths: the slowest case, needing the longest homogenisation.

6.html:
Why cryogenic treatment is essential

  1. Very low M_s and M_f. High-carbon high-chromium steels (D2, D3 type) put much carbon and Cr into the austenite, and both depress M_s and M_f far below room temperature. A normal quench therefore leaves a large amount of retained austenite (RA); Cr is one of the strongest RA formers (slide 46).
  2. RA is harmful in tools. It is soft, so hardness and wear resistance fall, and it is unstable: in service it slowly turns into brittle, untempered martensite with expansion, so dies and gauges change size and crack.
  3. Tempering alone is a poor cure. In high-alloy steels the RA survives tempering up to about 450^\circ\mathrm{C} and transforms only at 500 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C} (slide 55), which softens the matrix and needs several tempers.
  4. Cryotreatment (-135 to -196^\circ\mathrm{C}, 24 h) converts the RA and conditions the martensite: the defects it creates nucleate fine transition carbides on tempering. Tool life rises 2 to 5 times, size becomes stable and one temper is enough (slides 50-55).

M_s and tetragonal distortion

Given: 1.2% C and 6.0% Cr, all in solution after austenitising; no Mn given.

\begin{aligned} M_s &= 520 - 320(1.2) - 30(6.0) = 520 - 384 - 180 = -44^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ \frac{c}{a} &= 1 + 0.045(\mathrm{wt\%\,C}) = 1 + 0.045(1.2) = 1.054 \end{aligned}

The c axis of the BCT martensite is 5.4% longer than a (about 3.00 against 2.85 angstrom): very hard, brittle plate martensite that must be tempered.

M_s lies below room temperature, so a quench to 20^\circ\mathrm{C} gives practically no martensite. With f_M = 1 - \exp[-0.011(M_s - T)], cold treatment at -100^\circ\mathrm{C} gives only about 46% martensite, and liquid nitrogen at -196^\circ\mathrm{C} about 81%. This is why the cryogenic step is essential for this steel.

Answer: M_s \approx -44^\circ\mathrm{C}; c/a \approx 1.054, a tetragonal distortion of about 5.4%.

7.html:
A hardened part is soft when it contains too little martensite, or martensite with too little carbon, or when the martensite was later softened. The usual causes:

  1. Decarburisation. Heating in an oxidising atmosphere removes carbon from the surface, so the surface austenite holds less carbon and gives softer martensite (and lower hardenability). Remedy: machining allowance, protective atmosphere, salt bath or vacuum furnace.
  2. Under-heating or fast heating. Below A_3 a hypoeutectoid steel keeps proeutectoid ferrite, which stays soft after the quench: a mixed ferrite + martensite structure. Faulty thermocouples cause the same.
  3. Insufficient soaking. Carbides do not dissolve and the austenite is inhomogeneous, so less carbon and alloy are in solution; undissolved carbides sit in the martensite.
  4. Cooling slower than the critical cooling rate. Too mild a quenchant, a bath too small (it should be at least 5 times the work volume, recirculated), hot or water-contaminated oil, a slow transfer: the cooling curve cuts the nose and pearlite or bainite forms.
  5. Hardenability too low for the section. A plain carbon steel in a thick section hardens only at the skin; the core is fine pearlite (U-shaped hardness traverse).
  6. Retained austenite. Too high a hardening temperature in high-carbon steel dissolves excess carbon, lowering M_f below room temperature; delays during the quench stabilise it further. More than about 10% retained austenite lowers hardness markedly.
  7. Over-tempering. Too high a temperature or too long a time turns martensite into soft tempered martensite or ferrite + carbides.
  8. Soft spots: steam bubbles, scale or dirty surfaces give uneven hardness.

Also check the grade: a 0.2% C steel can never exceed about 45 HRC (35 + 50 \times 0.2).

8.html:
Why hardenability predicts hardness

The as-quenched hardness at any point depends on two things:

  1. Dissolved carbon, which sets the ceiling: the hardness of 99.9% martensite, 35 + 50(\%\mathrm{C}) HRC.
  2. The fraction of martensite at that point, which depends on whether the local cooling rate beats the steel's critical cooling rate.

The second is decided by hardenability (dissolved alloy and grain size, measured as D_I or a Jominy curve) together with the section size and the quench severity H. Carbon alone cannot predict hardness: 1040 and 4340 both have 0.4% C and reach about 57 HRC at the Jominy end, but 20 mm along, 1040 has fallen to about 20 HRC while 4340 still has over 50 HRC (slide 22). With D_I and H (Grossmann), or a Jominy curve and equivalent cooling-rate charts, the martensite fraction at the surface, mid-radius or centre is found first, and then the hardness from carbon and martensite content. Steels are selected on this basis before any part is made.

Here both parts have the same composition and austenitising, so the same carbon; only the cooling rate differs. Water (H \approx 1 to 1.5) cools faster than oil (H \approx 0.35 to 0.5), giving 90% against 50% martensite.

Expected hardness

Relations (slide 22): \mathrm{HRC_{90}} = 30 + 50(\%\mathrm{C}) and \mathrm{HRC_{50}} = 23 + 50(\%\mathrm{C}), valid up to about 0.6% C. Carbon is not printed; take a 0.40% C steel (1040 or 4140 class):

\begin{aligned} \text{water, 90\% M:}\quad \mathrm{HRC} &= 30 + 50(0.40) = 50 \\ \text{oil, 50\% M:}\quad \mathrm{HRC} &= 23 + 50(0.40) = 43 \end{aligned}

Answer: water quenched about 50 HRC, oil quenched about 43 HRC. In general the water-quenched part is 30 + 50\%\mathrm{C} and the oil-quenched part 23 + 50\%\mathrm{C}, always 7 HRC harder for water below 0.6% C; at 0.6% C and above they level off at about 60 and 53 HRC.

9.html:
Pack carburising

Solid-medium carburising of low-carbon steel (0.1 to 0.25% C).

  1. Packing: the parts are packed in a heat-resisting steel box with carburising compound, at least 50 mm apart and from the walls. Compound: charcoal 30 to 32%, coke 30 to 32%, \mathrm{BaCO_3} 10 to 12% (energiser), \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} 2 to 3%. The lid is sealed with fireclay; areas to stay soft are copper plated or clay covered.
  2. Heating: the box is heated to 900 to 950^\circ\mathrm{C}, where austenite dissolves much carbon, and held for several hours; case depth \approx K\sqrt{t}.
  3. Reactions:
\begin{aligned} \mathrm{BaCO_3} &\rightarrow \mathrm{BaO + CO_2} \\ \mathrm{CO_2 + C} &\rightarrow \mathrm{2CO} \\ \mathrm{2CO} &\rightarrow \mathrm{C_{(\gamma\text{-}Fe)} + CO_2} \end{aligned}

The \mathrm{CO_2} released at the steel reacts again with the charcoal, so CO is regenerated in a cycle; the energiser speeds it. The atomic carbon dissolves in austenite and diffuses inward.

  1. Case: carbon falls from the surface to the core. Slowly cooled, the zones are hypereutectoid (pearlite + cementite network), eutectoid (pearlite), hypoeutectoid (pearlite + ferrite) and the core (mostly ferrite).
  2. Finishing: the box is cooled and unpacked, and the parts are hardened (reheat and quench) and tempered at 150 to 180^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Gas carburising compared with pack

Advantages

  • Surface carbon and case depth are accurately controlled through the carbon potential (CO/\mathrm{CO_2}, dew point; boost-diffuse).
  • More uniform case.
  • Cleaner and more efficient: no compound to handle or dispose of.
  • Much shorter cycle: no box to heat, continuous carbon supply, direct quench possible.
  • Suits mass production and automation.

Disadvantages

  • Expensive furnace, gas generator and trays.
  • Needs greater operating skill and atmosphere control.
  • Fire, explosion and toxic CO hazards.
  • Internal (grain-boundary) oxidation and soot if the atmosphere is poorly controlled.
  • Uneconomical for small batches or single large parts, where pack is simpler.
